section: Ch 15 landing, Rosa Part 15
old: Her nurse practitioner adjusts her medicines until she can eat again. Her daughter notices a fruity smell on her breath.
new: Her daughter notices a fruity smell on her breath. Vomiting that will not stop, ketones and fruity breath are warning signs of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), so her plan says to get care right away. At the emergency department a blood test shows that her blood pH is normal: she has ketosis from not eating, not ketoacidosis (Section 15.5). She is given IV fluids, and her nurse practitioner adjusts her medicines until she can eat again.
reason: As written, a patient with diabetes who has vomited for two days, has moderate ketones and fruity breath is managed at home. CDC (the book's own source 1 in 15.5) lists fruity breath and vomiting with inability to keep food or drink down as reasons to go to the ER or call 911, and says DKA also occurs in type 2 diabetes. The rewrite keeps the chemistry (ketosis versus ketoacidosis, blood pH) and models the safe action. No dose or treatment advice added.

section: 7.12 Chapter Guide, Case Question 7.1 answer (occurs twice: inline answer and print key; change both)
old: The amine reacts with HCl to form an ammonium salt (R<sub>3</sub>NH<sup>+</sup> Cl<sup>−</sup>).
new: A basic nitrogen accepts H<sup>+</sup> from HCl to form a salt (for lidocaine’s amine, R<sub>3</sub>NH<sup>+</sup> Cl<sup>−</sup>; a basic nitrogen in metformin does the same).
